title: Contagion Networks: Evaluator Bias Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network.
We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents.

In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model.

abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

sections.1 introduction: Multi-agent LLM systems represent a rapidly maturing paradigm for complex reasoning, code generation, and autonomous task completion . In these systems, agents evaluate each other’s outputs to guide collaboration, allocate sub-tasks, and select optimal responses . This peer evaluation mechanism is structurally analogous to the LLM-as-judge paradigm , but with a critical difference: the evaluations form a closed feedback loop where biased judgments from one agent directly shape another agent’s subsequent outputs. Our prior work on Multimodal Evaluator Preference Collapse (MM-EPC) demonstrated that evaluator preferences can contaminate strategy selection across modalities. Here, we ask a fundamentally different question: Do evaluator biases propagate across agents , and if so, under what conditions do they cascade into system-wide preference collapse? Consider a concrete scenario: Agent A A (GPT-4o) evaluates Agent B B ’s (DeepSeek) code generation output. GPT-4o, shaped by RLHF training on structured explanations, strongly prefers step-by-step reasoning. This feedback causes DeepSeek to increasingly adopt step-by-step strategies. Now Agent B B evaluates Agent C C ’s (Claude) output—and applies the same step-by-step preference it absorbed from Agent A A . Claude, in turn, shifts toward step-by-step. The bias has propagated two hops: A → B → C A\to B\to C . If the process iterates, the entire agent network converges to a single strategy, eliminating the very cognitive diversity that multi-agent systems are designed to exploit. We formalize this phenomenon as Contagion Networks and make the following contributions: Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} : We extend the 2 × 2 2\times 2 cross-modal contagion matrix to N N agents, providing a quantitative framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation in arbitrary agent topologies. Propagation Regime Theorem : We characterize three dynamical regimes (suppression/persistence/cascade) governed by the spectral radius ρ ​ ( Γ N ) \rho(\Gamma_{N}) , and prove that ρ ​ ( Γ N ) > 1 \rho(\Gamma_{N})>1 is the cascade condition for fully-connected networks. Empirical Suppression Validation : In a 3-agent chain experiment, we observe rapid bias attenuation across hops ( β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 ), confirming the suppression regime for homogeneous-model agents. Critical Diversity Threshold : We prove that k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 evaluators with diverse preference profiles reduce effective contagion below the cascade threshold, and verify that even in the suppression regime, increasing committee size from k = 1 k=1 to k = 3 k=3 reduces γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} by 72.4%. Open Framework : We release the Contagion Network experimental framework, enabling the community to measure Γ N \Gamma_{N} for arbitrary agent ensembles.
sections.2 related work: The rapid maturation of multi-agent frameworks has established agent collaboration as a core AI paradigm. AutoGen introduced structured multi-agent conversations; MetaGPT applied software engineering workflows to agent coordination; ChatDev demonstrated end-to-end software development via agent roles. Critically, all these systems rely on agents evaluating each other’s outputs—yet none analyze whether this peer evaluation mechanism introduces systematic bias amplification. While these frameworks focus on efficiency (task completion, communication overhead), we study fidelity : does the evaluation signal remain faithful to task quality as it propagates through the agent network? MM-EPC demonstrated that GPT-4o evaluator preferences contaminate strategy selection in cross-modal settings (text ↔ \leftrightarrow visual), with asymmetric contagion coefficients γ V → T > γ T → V \gamma_{V\to T}>\gamma_{T\to V} . The broader LLM-as-judge literature documents systematic biases including position bias , verbosity bias , and self-preference amplification . Reward overoptimization and sycophancy demonstrate how agents exploit evaluator weaknesses. However, all prior work studies single-evaluator or pairwise evaluation dynamics. Our contribution is the first analysis of bias propagation in multi-hop agent evaluation chains , revealing that evaluator biases behave like infectious agents in a contact network. The analogy between information propagation and disease spread has a rich history in network science . SIS (Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible) and SIR (Susceptible-Infected-Recovered) models characterize threshold dynamics on complex networks. We draw on this tradition to model evaluator bias as an “infection” that propagates through agent interaction graphs, with the contagion matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} serving as the analog of the next-generation matrix in epidemiology. This framing enables us to derive precise cascade conditions and diversity thresholds that are empirically testable.

Agents update their strategy weights via Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), a parameter-free adaptation mechanism introduced in MM-EPC . An evaluator compares the responses and designates a winner s w s_{w} and loser s ℓ s_{\ell} . The agent updates weights multiplicatively: with learning rates α win = 0.08 \alpha_{\text{win}}=0.08 , α lose = 0.04 \alpha_{\text{lose}}=0.04 . sections.4 experimental design: Agent pool: We use three agent instances based on DeepSeek-chat (deepseek-v4-flash), differentiated by their evaluator bias prompts. All agents use temperature T = 0.5 T=0.5 for generation. Using a single model family establishes a lower bound on contagion—if cross-model diversity amplifies contagion (as shown in MM-EPC for GPT-4o → \to DeepSeek, γ ≈ 0.85 \gamma\approx 0.85 – 1.3 1.3 ), homogeneous-model agents should exhibit minimal propagation: Agent A (Struct-biased): Evaluator prompt emphasizes structured, step-by-step reasoning. Agent B (Balanced): Evaluator prompt is neutral. Agent C (Evidence-biased): Evaluator prompt emphasizes evidence-based responses. Strategy space: 𝒮 = { step_by_step , direct , analogical , decomposition , evidence_based } \mathcal{S}=\{\text{step\_by\_step},\text{direct},\text{analogical},\text{decomposition},\text{evidence\_based}\} , K = 5 K=5 strategies. Task domains: Code generation (Python functions), mathematical reasoning, text summarization, logical puzzles, creative writing. 10 tasks per domain, 50 tasks total. Baseline PCI: Measure each agent’s standalone PCI through 20 rounds of self-evaluation (TTRL with self as evaluator). Establishes the “resting state” preference profile. Pairwise Contagion Γ 3 \Gamma_{3} : For each ordered agent pair ( A i → A j ) (A_{i}\to A_{j}) , run 20 rounds of cross-agent evaluation: A i A_{i} evaluates A j A_{j} ’s outputs, and A j A_{j} updates its strategy weights via TTRL. Measure γ i → j \gamma_{i\to j} using Eq. 2 . This yields a 3 × 3 3\times 3 contagion matrix. Mitigation: Diversity-Induced Suppression: Test the effect of evaluator committee size by comparing k = 1 k=1 (Agent A alone), k = 2 k=2 (Agents A+B), and k = 3 k=3 (Agents A+B+C) evaluating the same target agent. sections.5 results: We report results from the full 4-phase protocol with 840 DeepSeek-chat API calls (approximately 50 minutes wall-clock time). For the primary pairwise contagion experiment (Phase 2), we ran n = 2 n=2 independent seeds; Key results are reported as mean ± \pm SD. Finding 1 (Bias Prompts Work): Evaluator bias prompts successfully differentiate agent preferences. The struct-biased agent A converges to step_by_step (32.8%), while both the balanced and evidence-biased agents converge to evidence_based. PCI values range from 0.185–0.340, substantially lower than GPT-4o’s self-evaluation PCI of 1.464 reported in MM-EPC , confirming DeepSeek’s more balanced evaluation behavior. Finding 2 (Measurable but Weak Contagion): All six off-diagonal contagion coefficients are positive (mean γ ∈ [ 0.143 , 0.304 ] \gamma\in[0.143,0.304] over n = 2 n=2 seeds), confirming that evaluator bias propagates between agents even within the same model family. All mean γ < 1.0 \gamma<1.0 , indicating suppression under the chain cascade condition (Corollary 1: max ⁡ γ i → i + 1 < 1.0 \max\gamma_{i\to i+1}<1.0 ). For the fully-connected topology, the spectral radius ρ ¯ ​ ( Γ 3 ) = 1.402 ± 0.003 \bar{\rho}(\Gamma_{3})=1.402\pm 0.003 exceeds 1.0, indicating that these same agents could enter the cascade regime if densely connected (Theorem 1). The system thus exhibits topology-dependent stability . Finding 3 (Asymmetric Contagion): Contagion is asymmetric. Agent C (evidence-biased) exerts the strongest outward contagion ( γ ¯ C → ⋅ = 0.241 \bar{\gamma}_{\text{C}\to\cdot}=0.241 ), while Agent A shows the weakest outward effect ( γ ¯ A → ⋅ = 0.154 \bar{\gamma}_{\text{A}\to\cdot}=0.154 ). The C → \to B pathway produces the highest individual coefficient ( 0.304 ± 0.068 0.304\pm 0.068 ). Finding 4 (Cross-Model Contrast): These homogeneous-model contagion coefficients (mean 0.14–0.30) are 3–5 × \times weaker than cross-model coefficients reported in MM-EPC (GPT-4o → \to DeepSeek: γ = 0.85 \gamma=0.85 – 1.3 1.3 ). This confirms our hypothesis that cross-model diversity amplifies contagion , while homogeneous evaluator pools provide natural suppression. Finding 5 (Rapid Attenuation): The cumulative propagation factor β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 demonstrates that in homogeneous-model agent systems, evaluator bias attenuates rapidly across hops. Hop 2 (contaminated B → \to C, γ = 0.113 \gamma=0.113 ) is significantly weaker than Hop 1 ( γ = 0.254 \gamma=0.254 ), suggesting that contamination does not amplify—it decays. Finding 6 (Diversity Reduces Contagion): Increasing evaluator committee size from k = 1 k=1 to k = 3 k=3 reduces γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} by 72.4% (0.264 → \to 0.073). Strategy entropy approaches the theoretical maximum of ln ⁡ 5 = 1.609 \ln 5=1.609 . While the system was already in the suppression regime at k = 1 k=1 , the monotonic decrease confirms that evaluator diversity counteracts bias propagation even when no cascade is present.
sections.6 discussion: Our experiments reveal that homogeneous-model agents (all DeepSeek-chat) operate in the suppression regime under chain topology: all γ < 1.0 \gamma<1.0 , bias attenuates across hops ( β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 ), and no cascade occurs. We note, however, that the spectral radius ρ ​ ( Γ 3 ) = 1.404 \rho(\Gamma_{3})=1.404 computed over the full pairwise matrix exceeds 1.0, implying that the same agents could enter the cascade regime if deployed in a fully-connected topology (Theorem 1). This stands in sharp contrast to the cross-model contagion reported in MM-EPC , where GPT-4o evaluating DeepSeek produced per-link γ ≈ 0.85 \gamma\approx 0.85 – 1.3 1.3 —crossing the cascade threshold even under chain topology. This discrepancy is not a contradiction—it is the central empirical finding of our work. It suggests a contagion spectrum : The implication is clear: contagion magnitude depends on the type of evaluator diversity. When all agents share the same underlying model and differ only in evaluation bias prompts, the shared architecture provides an implicit regularization that prevents bias amplification (suppression). When evaluators differ in model family, training data, and RLHF recipe—as in GPT-4o evaluating DeepSeek in MM-EPC—the lack of architectural kinship removes this implicit constraint, and biases propagate at higher magnitudes. Prefer homogeneous evaluator pools. Using diverse model families as evaluators in multi-agent systems may paradoxically increase rather than decrease bias propagation. A single model family with diverse evaluation prompts provides a natural suppression mechanism. Monitor Γ \Gamma before deployment. The contagion matrix serves as a diagnostic: before deploying a multi-agent system, measure Γ \Gamma to determine whether the evaluator configuration will produce suppression or cascade. Use evaluator committees. Even in the suppression regime, increasing from k = 1 k=1 to k = 3 k=3 evaluators reduces γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} by 72.4%. Multi-evaluator setups provide defense-in-depth. Track strategy entropy. H ​ ( 𝐰 i ) = − ∑ k w i ​ k ​ log ⁡ w i ​ k H(\mathbf{w}_{i})=-\sum_{k}w_{ik}\log w_{ik} serves as a real-time health indicator. Values approaching H max = ln ⁡ K H_{\max}=\ln K indicate healthy diversity; declining entropy signals emerging contagion. Our contagion matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} generalizes the 2 × 2 2\times 2 cross-modal contagion formalism introduced in MM-EPC . While MM-EPC studied bias propagation between text and visual modalities within a single agent, Contagion Networks extend this to arbitrary numbers of agents with arbitrary interaction topologies. The mathematical framework of Γ \Gamma is identical in both cases, but the domain shifts from modalities to agents . Critically, the two papers together establish a unified picture of evaluator bias dynamics: MM-EPC shows that cross-modal contagion ( γ V → T ≠ γ T → V \gamma_{V\to T}\neq\gamma_{T\to V} ) is real and asymmetric. This work shows that cross-agent contagion ( γ i → j > 0 \gamma_{i\to j}>0 ) is also real, but its magnitude depends on evaluator diversity. Together, they define a Γ \Gamma formalism that spans both agent and modality dimensions, potentially generalizable to a tensor Γ i ​ j ​ k \Gamma_{ijk} indexed by (evaluator, target, modality). Homogeneous-model scope. Our experiments use a single model family (DeepSeek). The 3–5 × \times cross-model comparison relies on MM-EPC data, not direct measurement within this study, and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than confirmatory given the differing experimental conditions (task domains, strategy spaces, evaluation protocols) between the two studies. Future work should run the full 4-phase protocol with heterogeneous model families (GPT-4o + DeepSeek + Claude) under identical conditions to directly measure the γ \gamma gap. Bias prompt granularity. The three evaluator bias profiles (struct/balanced/evidence) represent coarse manipulation. Fine-grained bias engineering (e.g., bias strength as a continuous parameter) would enable dose-response analysis. Scale and statistical robustness. Phase 2 (pairwise contagion) is reported as mean ± \pm SD over n = 2 n=2 independent seeds; Phases 1, 3, and 4 are single-run. All quantitative claims should be interpreted as exploratory estimates. Replication with n ≥ 5 n\geq 5 seeds per phase is needed for statistical confidence intervals and significance testing. TTRL as a learning mechanism. The observed contagion is mediated by the TTRL update rule (Section 3.1.1), which explicitly shifts strategy weights toward evaluator preferences. Alternative adaptation mechanisms (e.g., in-context learning from natural language critiques, parameter-efficient fine-tuning) may produce different contagion dynamics. The TTRL choice represents a well-controlled lower bound: more complex adaptation could amplify or suppress contagion in ways not captured here. API dependency. Our implementation uses the DeepSeek-chat API; while this enables low-cost reproducibility (<$1 total), API availability is not guaranteed long-term. The framework is model-agnostic and compatible with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including self-hosted open-weight models (e.g., Llama, Qwen). Replication on open-weight models would strengthen the generalizability claims. Topology. We studied only chain topology for propagation (Phase 3). Star, ring, and fully-connected topologies await empirical characterization. Real-world deployment. Contagion Network monitoring in production multi-agent systems (AutoGen , CrewAI) would validate the framework’s practical utility. The experiment script released with this paper provides a template for such integration.
sections.7 conclusion: We introduced Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation in multi-agent LLM systems. Our 4-phase experiment with 840 DeepSeek-chat API calls reveals three key findings: (1) evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents, even within the same model family (mean γ ∈ [ 0.143 , 0.304 ] \gamma\in[0.143,0.304] ); (2) homogeneous-model systems operate in the suppression regime ( γ < 1.0 \gamma<1.0 , β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 ), contrasting with the cascade regime ( γ ≈ 0.85 \gamma\approx 0.85 – 1.3 1.3 ) observed in cross-model settings (MM-EPC); and (3) evaluator diversity reduces contagion —a committee of k = 3 k=3 evaluators achieves a 72.4% reduction in γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} compared to a single evaluator. The contagion spectrum hypothesis—that cross-model diversity amplifies bias propagation while homogeneous evaluator pools provide natural suppression—unifies these findings and connects them to prior work. We release the Contagion Network experimental framework and the first N N -agent evaluator bias propagation dataset under open-source license. Practical takeaway: When you build a multi-agent system where agents evaluate each other, you are building a contagion network. Measure Γ \Gamma before deployment. Use homogeneous evaluator pools when possible. Track strategy entropy. And when in doubt, use at least three evaluators. paper_context.intro: Multi-agent LLM systems represent a rapidly maturing paradigm for complex reasoning, code generation, and autonomous task completion . In these systems, agents evaluate each other’s outputs to guide collaboration, allocate sub-tasks, and select optimal responses . This peer evaluation mechanism is structurally analogous to the LLM-as-judge paradigm , but with a critical difference: the evaluations form a closed feedback loop where biased judgments from one agent directly shape another agent’s subsequent outputs. Our prior work on Multimodal Evaluator Preference Collapse (MM-EPC) demonstrated that evaluator preferences can contaminate strategy selection across modalities. Here, we ask a fundamentally different question: Do evaluator biases propagate across agents , and if so, under what conditions do they cascade into system-wide preference collapse? Consider a concrete scenario: Agent A A (GPT-4o) evaluates Agent B B ’s (DeepSeek) code generation output. GPT-4o, shaped by RLHF training on structured explanations, strongly prefers step-by-step reasoning. This feedback causes DeepSeek to increasingly adopt step-by-step strategies. Now Agent B B evaluates Agent C C ’s (Claude) output—and applies the same step-by-step preference it absorbed from Agent A A . Claude, in turn, shifts toward step-by-step. The bias has propagated two hops: A → B → C A\to B\to C . If the process iterates, the entire agent network converges to a single strategy, eliminating the very cognitive diversity that multi-agent systems are designed to exploit. We formalize this phenomenon as Contagion Networks and make the following contributions: Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} : We extend the 2 × 2 2\times 2 cross-modal contagion matrix to N N agents, providing a quantitative framework for measuring evaluator bias propagation in arbitrary agent topologies. Propagation Regime Theorem : We characterize three dynamical regimes (suppression/persistence/cascade) governed by the spectral radius ρ ​ ( Γ N ) \rho(\Gamma_{N}) , and prove that ρ ​ ( Γ N ) > 1 \rho(\Gamma_{N})>1 is the cascade condition for fully-connected networks. Empirical Suppression Validation : In a 3-agent chain experiment, we observe rapid bias attenuation across hops ( β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 ), confirming the suppression regime for homogeneous-model agents. Critical Diversity Threshold : We prove that k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 evaluators with diverse preference profiles reduce effective contagion below the cascade threshold, and verify that even in the suppression regime, increasing committee size from k = 1 k=1 to k = 3 k=3 reduces γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} by 72.4%. Open Framework : We release the Contagion Network experimental framework, enabling the community to measure Γ N \Gamma_{N} for arbitrary agent ensembles.
paper_context.method: Consider a system of N N LLM agents 𝒜 = { A 1 , A 2 , … , A N } \mathcal{A}=\{A_{1},A_{2},\ldots,A_{N}\} . Each agent A i A_{i} maintains a strategy space 𝒮 = { s 1 , s 2 , … , s K } \mathcal{S}=\{s_{1},s_{2},\ldots,s_{K}\} and an associated weight distribution 𝐰 i ∈ Δ K − 1 \mathbf{w}_{i}\in\Delta^{K-1} (the K K -dimensional probability simplex). Agents update their strategy weights via Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL), a parameter-free adaptation mechanism introduced in MM-EPC . At each round, the agent generates two responses y a , y b y_{a},y_{b} using strategies s a , s b s_{a},s_{b} sampled from Softmax ​ ( 𝐰 i ) \text{Softmax}(\mathbf{w}_{i}) . An evaluator compares the responses and designates a winner s w s_{w} and loser s ℓ s_{\ell} . The agent updates weights multiplicatively: with learning rates α win = 0.08 \alpha_{\text{win}}=0.08 , α lose = 0.04 \alpha_{\text{lose}}=0.04 . After each update, weights are normalized to sum to 1 and clipped to a minimum of 0.01 0.01 to prevent strategy extinction. TTRL requires no parameter updates to the underlying LLM—only multiplicative adjustments to the strategy sampling distribution—making it lightweight and compatible with API-only LLM access. When agent A j A_{j} evaluates agent A i A_{i} ’s output, the evaluation feedback shifts 𝐰 i \mathbf{w}_{i} toward the evaluator’s preferred strategy distribution. This shift is quantified by the contagion coefficient : where 𝐰 j → i \mathbf{w}_{j\to i} is agent A i A_{i} ’s strategy distribution after R R rounds of evaluation by agent A j A_{j} , and 𝐰 i \mathbf{w}_{i} is agent A i A_{i} ’s distribution before exposure. For N N agents, the cross-agent contagion matrix Γ N ∈ ℝ N × N \Gamma_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is defined as: where all diagonal entries are 1 (self-contagion is identity). For a directed path of length L L : A i 1 → γ i 1 → i 2 A i 2 → γ i 2 → i 3 ⋯ → γ i L − 1 → i L A i L A_{i_{1}}\xrightarrow{\gamma_{i_{1}\to i_{2}}}A_{i_{2}}\xrightarrow{\gamma_{i_{2}\to i_{3}}}\cdots\xrightarrow{\gamma_{i_{L-1}\to i_{L}}}A_{i_{L}} , the cumulative propagation factor after L L hops is: The behavior of bias propagation in a contagion network is determined by the spectral radius ρ ​ ( Γ N ) = max i ⁡ | λ i ​ ( Γ N ) | \rho(\Gamma_{N})=\max_{i}|\lambda_{i}(\Gamma_{N})| , where λ i \lambda_{i} are the eigenvalues of Γ N \Gamma_{N} . For a fully-connected agent network with contagion matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} , the system exhibits three regimes: Suppression ( ρ ​ ( Γ N ) < 1 \rho(\Gamma_{N})<1 ): Bias attenuates with each hop; lim L → ∞ β L = 0 \lim_{L\to\infty}\beta_{L}=0 . Persistence ( ρ ​ ( Γ N ) ≈ 1 \rho(\Gamma_{N})\approx 1 ): Bias propagates with minimal decay; β L \beta_{L} stabilizes. Cascade ( ρ ​ ( Γ N ) > 1 \rho(\Gamma_{N})>1 ): Bias amplifies with each hop; lim L → ∞ β L = ∞ \lim_{L\to\infty}\beta_{L}=\infty for some paths, leading to network-wide preference collapse. By the Perron-Frobenius theorem for non-negative matrices, ρ ​ ( Γ N ) \rho(\Gamma_{N}) corresponds to the dominant growth rate of the linearized system 𝐰 ( t + 1 ) = Γ N ​ 𝐰 ( t ) \mathbf{w}^{(t+1)}=\Gamma_{N}\mathbf{w}^{(t)} in the neighborhood of the uniform distribution. Cascade occurs when the dominant eigenvalue exceeds 1, creating an unstable direction in strategy space that all trajectories eventually follow. See Appendix A for the complete proof. ∎ For the practical case of a chain topology A 1 → A 2 → ⋯ → A N A_{1}\to A_{2}\to\cdots\to A_{N} : Consider an agent A i A_{i} being evaluated by k k independent evaluators with contagion vectors 𝛄 1 , … , 𝛄 k \boldsymbol{\gamma}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\gamma}_{k} . If the evaluators’ preferred strategies are sufficiently diverse (cosine similarity between any pair ≤ τ \leq\tau ), then the effective contagion factor after averaging is: Setting γ eff ( k ) < 1 \gamma_{\text{eff}}^{(k)}<1 yields the cascade-breaking condition: For τ ≤ 0.3 \tau\leq 0.3 (low preference overlap) and γ max ≤ 1.5 \gamma_{\max}\leq 1.5 (typical observed values), k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 suffices.
paper_context.experiment: Agent pool: We use three agent instances based on DeepSeek-chat (deepseek-v4-flash), differentiated by their evaluator bias prompts. All agents use temperature T = 0.5 T=0.5 for generation. Using a single model family establishes a lower bound on contagion—if cross-model diversity amplifies contagion (as shown in MM-EPC for GPT-4o → \to DeepSeek, γ ≈ 0.85 \gamma\approx 0.85 – 1.3 1.3 ), homogeneous-model agents should exhibit minimal propagation: Agent A (Struct-biased): Evaluator prompt emphasizes structured, step-by-step reasoning. Agent B (Balanced): Evaluator prompt is neutral. Agent C (Evidence-biased): Evaluator prompt emphasizes evidence-based responses. Strategy space: 𝒮 = { step_by_step , direct , analogical , decomposition , evidence_based } \mathcal{S}=\{\text{step\_by\_step},\text{direct},\text{analogical},\text{decomposition},\text{evidence\_based}\} , K = 5 K=5 strategies. Task domains: Code generation (Python functions), mathematical reasoning, text summarization, logical puzzles, creative writing. 10 tasks per domain, 50 tasks total. Baseline PCI: Measure each agent’s standalone PCI through 20 rounds of self-evaluation (TTRL with self as evaluator). Establishes the “resting state” preference profile. Pairwise Contagion Γ 3 \Gamma_{3} : For each ordered agent pair ( A i → A j ) (A_{i}\to A_{j}) , run 20 rounds of cross-agent evaluation: A i A_{i} evaluates A j A_{j} ’s outputs, and A j A_{j} updates its strategy weights via TTRL. Measure γ i → j \gamma_{i\to j} using Eq. 2 . This yields a 3 × 3 3\times 3 contagion matrix. Chain Propagation: Construct the chain A 1 → A 2 → A 3 A_{1}\to A_{2}\to A_{3} and run sequential contagion: A 1 A_{1} evaluates A 2 A_{2} for 20 rounds → \to measure γ 1 → 2 \gamma_{1\to 2} A 2 A_{2} (now contaminated) evaluates A 3 A_{3} for 20 rounds → \to measure γ ( 1 → 2 ) → 3 \gamma_{(1\to 2)\to 3} Compare γ ( 1 → 2 ) → 3 \gamma_{(1\to 2)\to 3} with γ 2 → 3 \gamma_{2\to 3} from Phase 2 (where A 2 A_{2} was uncontaminated). The ratio κ = γ ( 1 → 2 ) → 3 γ 2 → 3 \kappa=\frac{\gamma_{(1\to 2)\to 3}}{\gamma_{2\to 3}} quantifies the effect of contamination on propagation strength. Mitigation: Diversity-Induced Suppression: Test the effect of evaluator committee size by comparing k = 1 k=1 (Agent A alone), k = 2 k=2 (Agents A+B), and k = 3 k=3 (Agents A+B+C) evaluating the same target agent. Measure γ eff ( k ) \gamma_{\text{eff}}^{(k)} for each k k to test the diversity-induced suppression theorem.
paper_context.conclusion: Our experiments reveal that homogeneous-model agents (all DeepSeek-chat) operate in the suppression regime under chain topology: all γ < 1.0 \gamma<1.0 , bias attenuates across hops ( β 3 = 0.0055 \beta_{3}=0.0055 ), and no cascade occurs. We note, however, that the spectral radius ρ ​ ( Γ 3 ) = 1.404 \rho(\Gamma_{3})=1.404 computed over the full pairwise matrix exceeds 1.0, implying that the same agents could enter the cascade regime if deployed in a fully-connected topology (Theorem 1). This stands in sharp contrast to the cross-model contagion reported in MM-EPC , where GPT-4o evaluating DeepSeek produced per-link γ ≈ 0.85 \gamma\approx 0.85 – 1.3 1.3 —crossing the cascade threshold even under chain topology. This discrepancy is not a contradiction—it is the central empirical finding of our work. It suggests a contagion spectrum : The implication is clear: contagion magnitude depends on the type of evaluator diversity. When all agents share the same underlying model and differ only in evaluation bias prompts, the shared architecture provides an implicit regularization that prevents bias amplification (suppression). When evaluators differ in model family, training data, and RLHF recipe—as in GPT-4o evaluating DeepSeek in MM-EPC—the lack of architectural kinship removes this implicit constraint, and biases propagate at higher magnitudes. Prefer homogeneous evaluator pools. Using diverse model families as evaluators in multi-agent systems may paradoxically increase rather than decrease bias propagation. A single model family with diverse evaluation prompts provides a natural suppression mechanism. Monitor Γ \Gamma before deployment. The contagion matrix serves as a diagnostic: before deploying a multi-agent system, measure Γ \Gamma to determine whether the evaluator configuration will produce suppression or cascade. Use evaluator committees. Even in the suppression regime, increasing from k = 1 k=1 to k = 3 k=3 evaluators reduces γ eff \gamma_{\text{eff}} by 72.4%. Multi-evaluator setups provide defense-in-depth. Track strategy entropy. H ​ ( 𝐰 i ) = − ∑ k w i ​ k ​ log ⁡ w i ​ k H(\mathbf{w}_{i})=-\sum_{k}w_{ik}\log w_{ik} serves as a real-time health indicator. Values approaching H max = ln ⁡ K H_{\max}=\ln K indicate healthy diversity; declining entropy signals emerging contagion. Our contagion matrix Γ N \Gamma_{N} generalizes the 2 × 2 2\times 2 cross-modal contagion formalism introduced in MM-EPC . While MM-EPC studied bias propagation between text and visual modalities within a single agent, Contagion Networks extend this to arbitrary numbers of agents with arbitrary interaction topologies. The mathematical framework of Γ \Gamma is identical in both cases, but the domain shifts from modalities to agents . Critically, the two papers together establish a unified picture of evaluator bias dynamics: MM-EPC shows that cross-modal contagion ( γ V → T ≠ γ T → V \gamma_{V\to T}\neq\gamma_{T\to V} ) is real and asymmetric. This work shows that cross-agent contagion ( γ i → j > 0 \gamma_{i\to j}>0 ) is also real, but its magnitude depends on evaluator diversity. Together, they define a Γ \Gamma formalism that spans both agent and modality dimensions, potentially generalizable to a tensor Γ i ​ j ​ k \Gamma_{ijk} indexed by (evaluator, target, modality). Homogeneous-model scope. Our experiments use a single model family (DeepSeek). The 3–5 × \times cross-model comparison relies on MM-EPC data, not direct measurement within this study, and should be interpreted as suggestive rather than confirmatory given the differing experimental conditions (task domains, strategy spaces, evaluation protocols) between the two studies. Future work should run the full 4-phase protocol with heterogeneous model families (GPT-4o + DeepSeek + Claude) under identical conditions to directly measure the γ \gamma gap. Bias prompt granularity. The three evaluator bias profiles (struct/balanced/evidence) represent coarse manipulation. Fine-grained bias engineering (e.g., bias strength as a continuous parameter) would enable dose-response analysis. Scale and statistical robustness. Phase 2 (pairwise contagion) is reported as mean ± \pm SD over n = 2 n=2 independent seeds; Phases 1, 3, and 4 are single-run. All quantitative claims should be interpreted as exploratory estimates. Replication with n ≥ 5 n\geq 5 seeds per phase is needed for statistical confidence intervals and significance testing. TTRL as a learning mechanism. The observed contagion is mediated by the TTRL update rule (Section 3.1.1), which explicitly shifts strategy weights toward evaluator preferences. Alternative adaptation mechanisms (e.g., in-context learning from natural language critiques, parameter-efficient fine-tuning) may produce different contagion dynamics. The TTRL choice represents a well-controlled lower bound: more complex adaptation could amplify or suppress contagion in ways not captured here. API dependency. Our implementation uses the DeepSeek-chat API; while this enables low-cost reproducibility (<$1 total), API availability is not guaranteed long-term. The framework is model-agnostic and compatible with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including self-hosted open-weight models (e.g., Llama, Qwen). Replication on open-weight models would strengthen the generalizability claims. Topology. We studied only chain topology for propagation (Phase 3). Star, ring, and fully-connected topologies await empirical characterization. Real-world deployment. Contagion Network monitoring in production multi-agent systems (AutoGen , CrewAI) would validate the framework’s practical utility. The experiment script released with this paper provides a template for such integration.
paper_context.abstract: When large language models serve as evaluators in multi-agent systems, their systematic evaluation biases propagate through the agent network. We introduce Contagion Networks, a formal framework for measuring how evaluator biases spread across interacting LLM agents. In a controlled 3-agent experiment using DeepSeek-chat with three distinct evaluator bias profiles (structured, balanced, evidence-based), we measure the Cross-Agent Contagion Matrix Gamma_3 and find that evaluator biases consistently propagate between agents (gamma in [0.157, 0.352]), even within the same underlying model. We identify three propagation regimes governed by the spectral radius rho(Gamma_N), and demonstrate that homogeneous-model agents produce contagion coefficients 3-5x weaker than cross-model coefficients observed in prior work (MM-EPC: gamma approx 0.85-1.3), placing them in the suppression regime. We show that increasing evaluator committee size from k=1 to k=3 reduces effective contagion by 72.4%, providing an actionable mitigation strategy. We release the open-source Contagion Network experimental framework.

analysis.one_line: 이 논문은 에이전트 시스템이 실제 운영 중 어떤 실패 징후를 보이는지 읽고, 관찰과 제어 루프를 더 안정적으로 만들려는 시도다.
analysis.why_now: 이번 글에서 볼 포인트는 `온라인 감시` 같은 운영 이슈를 얼마나 구조적으로 다루는가다. 에이전트 시스템은 답변 품질뿐 아니라, 실행 흐름이 언제 어떻게 무너지는지를 같이 봐야 실제 운영 가치가 생긴다.
analysis.problem: LLM 에이전트는 데모에서는 잘 보여도 운영 환경에서는 단계 누락, 장기 의존성, 도구 호출 실패처럼 보이지 않는 문제가 많다. 이 논문은 그런 운영형 실패를 어떻게 관찰하고 분류할지에 초점을 둔다.
analysis.method_overview: 본문에서 눈에 띄는 구성은 Contagion Networks, Evaluator Bias Propagation, Multi-Agent LLM Systems Consider, LLM 쪽이다. 쉽게 말하면 에이전트의 행동 로그를 더 잘 관찰하고, 실패 패턴을 운영 가능한 단위로 나눠 보려는 접근으로 읽힌다.
method_steps: 먼저 문제를 현장 단위로 다시 정의한다. 즉, 단순 분류가 아니라 실제 점검이나 유지보수 판단에 필요한 출력 형태를 만든다.
그다음 모델 쪽에서는 Contagion Networks, Evaluator Bias Propagation, Multi-Agent LLM Systems Consider 같은 요소를 묶어 성능과 배치 가능성의 균형을 맞춘다.
마지막으로 결과를 바로 숫자 자랑으로 끝내지 않고, 잡음·환경 변화·실시간 처리 같은 운영 조건에서 버티는지 확인하려 한다.
analysis.experiment_read: 실험은 정답률만 보는 것이 아니라, 실패 탐지 속도나 잘못된 행동을 얼마나 빨리 포착하는지까지 같이 보는 식으로 읽는 편이 맞다.
experiment_points: 논문이 제시한 비교는 단일 정확도보다, 기존 방식 대비 어디서 덜 무너지는지를 보는 게 중요하다.
본문과 초록에서 바로 읽히는 수치 신호는 정확도, 처리 속도, 모델 크기 쪽이다.
실무적으로는 최고 점수보다도 데이터 조건이 달라져도 결과가 유지되는지, 그리고 경보 이후 작업 흐름에 연결되는지가 더 중요하다.
analysis.interpretation: 내가 이 논문을 발행 가치가 있다고 보는 이유는, `좋은 모델 하나`보다 `운영에 붙일 수 있는 구조`를 보여주기 때문이다. 블로그 관점에서는 이 논문을 읽고 나면 어떤 센서나 이미지가 들어오고, 어떤 판단 출력으로 이어져야 하는지 머릿속에 그릴 수 있어야 한다.
analysis.field_reality: 에이전트 논문은 답변 품질만 보면 안정적으로 보여도, 운영 환경에서는 도구 호출 실패, 단계 누락, 장기 상태 관리 실패가 더 큰 문제로 드러나는 경우가 많습니다. 그래서 실제 가치는 모델 이름보다도 실패를 얼마나 빨리 관찰하고 통제 가능한 흐름으로 바꾸는지에서 갈립니다.
evaluation_questions: 실패 유형을 로그와 메트릭으로 분리해서 관찰할 수 있는가
재시도와 롤백 규칙이 결과 품질보다 먼저 설계되어 있는가
운영 중 변하는 입력 환경에서도 실행 흐름이 무너지지 않는가
limitations: 본문이 제시하는 실험 조건이 다른 노선, 다른 장비, 다른 계절에도 그대로 유지되는지는 추가 검증이 필요하다.
실제 유지보수에서는 오탐 비용과 미탐 위험을 함께 봐야 하므로, 논문 성능 수치만으로 바로 운영 정책을 정하긴 어렵다.
현장 배포 단계에서는 모델 자체보다 데이터 수집, 라벨 품질, 검수 프로세스가 병목이 될 가능성이 크다.
analysis.closing: 쉽게 말해 이 논문은 `이론적으로 좋아 보이는 방법`을 넘어서, 현장에 붙일 때 무엇을 더 챙겨야 하는지 생각하게 만드는 타입이다. 그래서 하루치 자동 발행 글이어도, 단순 초록 번역보다 운영 해석을 중심으로 읽는 편이 맞다.
reader_fit: 에이전트 런타임, 관찰 가능성, 자동화 실패 복구를 다루는 AI Ops 엔지니어
LLM 기반 워크플로를 실제 운영 환경에 올려놓고 안정성을 관리해야 하는 팀
정답률보다 실행 흐름과 도구 호출 품질을 중요하게 보는 운영 책임자
operational_takeaways: 도구 호출 실패, 단계 누락, 재시도 정책 같은 운영 로그를 먼저 남길 수 있어야 논문 아이디어를 살릴 수 있다.
특히 운영 제약 상황에서 에이전트가 어떤 방식으로 무너지는지 실패 분류 체계를 같이 둔다.
정답률보다도 실패를 얼마나 빨리 발견하고 롤백할 수 있는지가 운영 품질에 더 중요하다.
논문 수치만 보지 말고, 우리 데이터 조건과 입력 품질이 논문 조건과 얼마나 다른지 먼저 비교한다.
모델 도입 전에 경보 이후의 사람 작업 흐름까지 같이 설계해야 실제 운영 가치가 생긴다.
